rv.q: Its cinematic staging creates a gloriously detailed shop-world that’s gradually dismantled, piece by piece, to leave only desolation.
Though the piece is slow to start and overwritten in places, it is at heart a tender piece about love and loss.
For me, though, the play's emotional impact is weakened by its whimsy.
Ed Thomas's Welsh play is a cheekily slight post-apocalyptic fantasy.
Despite committed performances and the magnetism of Ifans, the short evening winds up being as cold, woolly and unmoving as a sheep trapped in a snow-drift.
To me, it's a big 'no': a clunky bit of poeticism in a wearyingly obscure play heavy on intimations of profundity, but light on anything actually happening.
Rhys Ifans's tragicomic masterclass...Despite its rather abstract quality, 'On Bear Ridge' has enormous symbolic resonance.'
On Bear Ridge is a slow show and at times the unending tranquillity saddles the tragedy.
On Bear Ridge made me want to like it more than I did.

On Bear Ridge by Ed Thomas proclaims its amateurish origins with stage directions that belong in Pseuds Corner. ‘Spindly winter branches dance on a fading sign,’ is Thomas’s attempt to create a ghostly mood. The setting is a derelict village shop where ‘ancient bluebottles cling to death on sticky brown fly-catching strips’.
On Bear Ridge is, quite simply, a thing of beauty.
The script is rich in language and content, supported by excellent performances and a beautiful set.
Yet the writing simply isn’t strong enough to anchor such wayward suggestiveness in anything solid, despite being co-directed with flair by Vicky Featherstone.

cn.t: This post-apocalyptic Welsh drama divides critics with its Beckettian style and poetic ambiguity. Ifans and Ayola earn praise, but some find it beguiling while others deem it frustratingly obscure and slow.
